name: Expert System
analogy: Think of it as a veteran trader's rulebook written on index cards, with a clerk who reads the day's facts and pulls every card that applies. The clerk never gets tired, never forgets a card, and can always show which cards were used.

steps.title: Write the expert's knowledge as if-then rules
steps.description: A domain expert's rules of thumb are written as plain if-then statements and stored apart from the machinery that applies them. Each rule can carry a certainty number saying how far to trust it.
steps.inExample: Rule one, certainty 70 percent: if it is the New York open and volume is more than 50 percent above its average, the setup is good. Rule two, certainty 80 percent: if the setup is good and price is above a rising 50-bar average, enter long.

steps.title: Keep a board of current facts
steps.description: The system holds a working list of what is known right now. It grows as new readings arrive and as rules add conclusions of their own.
steps.inExample: Known facts are New York open, volume 80 percent above average, price above its rising 50-bar average, last 3 bars closed higher, and no news in the next 90 minutes.

steps.title: Find the rules whose conditions are met
steps.description: The engine compares every rule's conditions with the facts. In forward chaining it starts from the facts and moves toward conclusions; in backward chaining it starts from a goal and looks for support.
steps.inExample: Rules one and four match the facts straight away; rule two will match once a rule has added the fact that the setup is good; the news rule never matches because no release is near.

steps.title: Decide which rule fires first
steps.description: When several rules apply at once, a conflict-resolution strategy picks the order, for example the most specific rule first or the one with the freshest facts.
steps.inExample: Rule one fires first because it has more conditions, then rule four, and on the next cycle rule two.

steps.title: Combine certainties
steps.description: Each fired rule adds its conclusion to the board with a certainty. Two rules supporting the same conclusion strengthen it, and a conclusion that depends on another is weakened by multiplying by the rule's own certainty.
steps.inExample: Rule one (70 percent) and rule four (50 percent) both say the setup is good, which combine to 85 percent. Rule two then takes 80 percent of that 85 percent, a long entry at 68 percent.

steps.title: Give the answer with the rules used
steps.description: The system outputs its recommendation and the list of rules that fired, so a person can check each step against what they believe.
steps.inExample: The recommendation is a long entry with certainty 68 percent, listing rules one, four and two.

useFor.task: Turning a trader's habits into code
useFor.example: Capturing a discretionary trader's rules about the New York open, volume and confirmation bars so they run the same way every day.

useFor.task: Checks before an order goes out
useFor.example: Blocking a trade that breaks a stated risk rule, such as no entries within 5 minutes of a scheduled release.

useFor.task: Scoring a setup from several confirmations
useFor.example: Combining separate confirmation rules on an MNQ breakout into one certainty number.

useFor.task: A final sanity check on a learned model
useFor.example: Reviewing a model's long signal against a short rulebook and flagging disagreements for a human.

avoidWhen: The knowledge cannot be put into rules, because patterns hidden in 151 indicators are better found by a learned model such as gradient boosting.
Rules would need constant retuning as the market changes; a learned model refit on new bars adapts, while a rulebook waits for a human to update it.

example.scenario: At 09:40 on an MNQ 5-minute chart, the desk's rulebook is asked whether a long breakout entry is acceptable.

input.summary: Five current facts on the board and the four rules that apply to them.

fields.name: session
fields.meaning: Which part of the trading day the bar belongs to.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading is compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: price against its 50-bar moving average
fields.meaning: The fact used by the entry rule, rule two.

fields.name: last three bars
fields.meaning: The fact used by the confirmation rule, rule four, which says the setup is good with certainty 50 percent.

fields.name: minutes to next scheduled news
fields.meaning: The news-avoidance rule, rule three, only fires when this is under 15 minutes.

fields.name: rules in the rulebook
fields.meaning: Setup rule, entry rule, news rule and confirmation rule.

output.summary: A recommendation with a combined certainty and the rules that produced it.

fields.name: setup is good
fields.meaning: Two supporting rules combined: 70 percent and 50 percent.

fields.name: recommendation
fields.meaning: The setup certainty of 85 percent multiplied by the entry rule's own certainty of 80 percent.

fields.name: rules that fired
fields.meaning: Rules one, four and two fired; the news rule stayed silent because the release is 90 minutes away.

example.reading: A 68 percent recommendation with a visible chain is a prompt to look, not a command. Check the three fired rules against what you see on the chart, and remember that the certainties are the desk's own estimates and have not been measured on data.
